beats.intro: Module ten. [[sub]]Where a bond's return comes from, and why the investment horizon matters.
beats.sources: A fixed-rate bond has three sources of return. [[a]]First, the coupon and principal payments. [[b]]Second, the reinvestment of the coupons, which earns interest on interest. [[c]]Third, any gain or loss when the bond is sold before maturity. [[d]]The annualized return over the holding period is the horizon yield. [[e]]It equals the yield to maturity only if the bond is held to maturity, there is no default, and coupons are reinvested at that same yield.
beats.buy: Take a ten year bond with a six point two percent annual coupon, bought at par. [[vfo]]A buy-and-hold investor reinvests the coupons at six point two percent. The coupons add up to sixty two, but their future value is eighty two point four nine three. [[ioi]]The extra twenty point four nine three is interest on interest. [[ret]]With the principal, the investor ends with one hundred eighty two point four nine, and the annual return is exactly six point two percent, the yield to maturity.
beats.scen: Now rates change right after purchase. Two investors hold the bond. Viswan holds it ten years. Baywhite sells after four. [[flat]]If rates stay at six point two percent, both earn six point two. [[up]]If rates rise one point, the buy-and-hold investor gains from reinvesting at seven point two percent, and earns six point four three. [[upb]]Baywhite also reinvests at the higher rate, but sells at ninety five point two six three, a capital loss. Its return falls to five point two eight. [[dn]]If rates fall one point, the buy-and-hold investor earns only five point nine eight, because of lower reinvestment. [[dnb]]Baywhite sells at one hundred five point oh four three, and earns seven point one six. [[end]]Same bond, different horizons, opposite results.
beats.risks: Two risks pull in opposite directions. [[re]]Reinvestment risk: when rates fall, coupons are reinvested at lower rates. When rates rise, reinvestment helps. [[pr]]Price risk: when rates rise, the bond's sale price falls. [[hor]]The longer the horizon, the more reinvestment matters. The shorter the horizon, the more price risk matters. [[eq]]At one horizon, after about seven point seven years for this bond, the two effects cancel.
beats.mac: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time until a bond's cash flows arrive. [[w]]Each cash flow's weight is its share of the bond's price. [[ex]]For the ten year bond, the early coupons carry small weights, and the final payment carries more than half. [[val]]The Macaulay duration is seven point seven four years. It is the balance point. [[gap]]If the horizon equals the Macaulay duration, reinvestment risk and price risk offset. If the horizon is longer, reinvestment risk dominates. If it is shorter, price risk dominates.
beats.carry: A bond's price drifts toward par as it ages, if its yield does not change. [[traj]]Take a five year, three point two percent bond, bought at ninety six point four one, to yield four percent. Its constant-yield price trajectory rises toward one hundred. [[carry]]This is the carrying value: the purchase price, plus the amortized discount. [[gain]]If the bond is sold above the trajectory, there is a capital gain. Below it, a capital loss. [[int]]The drift toward par itself is part of interest income, not a gain.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Returns come from coupons, reinvestment, and gains or losses on sale. [[w2]]The horizon yield equals the yield to maturity only under three conditions. [[w3]]Reinvestment risk and price risk offset each other, and the horizon decides which wins. [[w4]]Macaulay duration is the horizon at which the two risks balance.
